newsitem.title: UK: UK GDP data suggest rates on hold until election.
newsitem.headline: UK GDP data suggest rates on hold until election.

text.p: Steady but unspectactular UK economic growth in the fourth quarter suggests Chancellor Kenneth Clarke will feel justified in keeping interest rates on hold until the election, analysts said on Monday.

"The latest data suggest the economy ended last year and started this year with less momentum than expected. The GDP figures are consistent with that and probably take the pressure off rates for now," said Robert Barrie, UK economist at BZW.
GDP grew 0.8 percent in the fourth quarter for year-on-year growth of 2.6 percent, bang in line with City forecasts.
Fourth quarter growth was just above the trend rate, estimated at around 2.5 percent.
But the Office for National Statistics estimated annual growth in 1996 below trend at 2.3 percent.
Barrie forecasts interest rates will stay on hold until the election, which must be held by May, unless the pound embarks on another downward slide.

Sterling's appreciation during the autumn was singled out by Clarke as a key factor behind his decision not to raise rates in January. But last week the rally came to an abrupt halt and the pound has lost over eight pfennigs since Tuesday.

Ian Stewart, UK economist at Merrill Lynch, agreed the GDP data make a pre-election rate rise most unlikely. "After these figures we certainly won't see a rate rise next Wednesday, and it is rather unlikely we'll see one this side of the election."
The next monetary meeting is on February 5.

Stewart said Bank of England Governor Eddie George will continue to press for a tightening, forcing Clarke to overrule him. "The Bank will carry on with the same line. The Governor has dug in heavily for pre-emptive rise, although he says only modest increase is needed."

But he said it is to close to an election for the government to tighten policy. "The Conservatives have tended to cut rates on the run up to elections so precedent suggests they are somewhat unlikely to raise them at this stage."
A breakdown of the data confirms the pattern of sluggish manufacturing activity and lively service sector growth continued in the fourth quarter.

The ONS said service output grew 0.9 percent on the quarter for year-on-year growth of 3.4 percent, while manufacturing output is estimated to have grown at a similar rate to the third quarter, which saw growth of 0.7 percent.
"The manufacturing sector is clearly wilting under pressure from currency strength," said Alex Garrard, UK economist at UBS.
"But output in the production industries overall grew by more than in the third quarter, mainly due to energy extraction and supply."
The ONS estimated construction grew far in excess of the third quarter, which saw just 0.4 percent growth.
